newsitem.title: GERMANY: CIA satellite photos showed Soviet Cold War ability.
newsitem.headline: CIA satellite photos showed Soviet Cold War ability.

text.p: U.S. satellite photographs given to Germany on the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall showed how Western intelligence experts were able to analyse the Soviet troop build-up around West Berlin during the Cold War.

Pictures taken by the Corona spy-in-the-sky from 1960 to 1972 also showed that Moscow did not have the military strength to launch a missile strike on the West, Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer Brian Latell told an audience on Saturday night.
The photographs show every item on the ground larger than five feet (two metres) across, Latell said at Berlin's America House, a cultural centre supported by the U.S. embassy.

Presenting enlargements of three photographs taken in May 1965 to Berlin's Allied Museum, he said the satellite's pictures had dispelled the West's fears of a "missile gap" -- the fear the Soviets were ahead in the arms race.
"The missile gap evaporated as an issue once Corona started taking pictures," said Latell, director of the CIA's Centre for the Study of Intelligence.
"The Soviet Union was not far ahead of the West in terms of strategic military capability."

Though the top U.S. priority was to use the information to assess Soviet ballistic millile bases and nuclear capability, other pictures clearly show the situation around West Berlin, then an enclave of democracy trapped behind the Iron Curtain.
Latell said it was always easier to assess the physical capabilities of the Soviets than to guess their intentions.

This meant that especially after the 1948-49 blockade when Moscow sealed access to West Berlin, the allies did not know whether the Soviets would next launch an offensive on the West or whether they would choose a defensive strategy.
The photographs of Berlin clearly show town centre landmarks such as the Brandenburg Gate and the Potsdamer Platz.

But they are only a detail of pictures which covered miles of northern Germany and western Poland. Corona took more than 80,000 photographs during its 12 years of operation and used more than two million feet of film.

Historians estimate that 90,000 heavily-armed Soviet troops were stationed within 32 km (20 miles) of West Berlin, largely outnumbering the 12,000 Western Allied troops. In Communist East Germany there were 338,000 Soviet troops.

Helmut Trotnow, director of the museum, said photographs taken by Corona in 1968 also showed Soviet tanks moving out of their barracks before the "Prague Spring" -- the democratic uprising in Czechoslovakia of that year.
"The tank movements could have been an exercise, nobody would have known what it meant at the time," he added.
As for developments in Berlin, although building materials would have been visible on the ground in the pictures, nobody knew the Soviets were planning to build a wall, Trotnow said.
